subtopics: Inversion of control and dependency injection
misconceptions: @Repository is only a naming convention with no behaviour of its own
Field injection is the recommended way to inject dependencies
Calling an annotated method from the same class still goes through the Spring proxy
A singleton bean is one instance per JVM

templates.subtopic: Inversion of control and dependency injection
templates.question: Explain dependency injection and inversion of control. Why does Spring recommend constructor injection over field injection?
keyPoints: With inversion of control the container creates the objects and wires their dependencies, instead of each object creating its own
Dependency injection supplies dependencies from outside, which decouples a class from concrete implementations and lets tests pass mocks
Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit and mandatory and allows final fields
A class with constructor injection can be created in a plain unit test without the container; field injection hides dependencies and needs reflection
With constructor injection a circular dependency fails at startup instead of being hidden

templates.question: What happens when a Spring Boot application starts, from SpringApplication.run until it is ready to serve requests?
keyPoints: SpringApplication prepares the Environment (property sources, active profiles) and creates the ApplicationContext
Component scanning from the package of the @SpringBootApplication class registers bean definitions
Auto-configuration classes are applied conditionally (@ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnProperty), so your own beans take precedence
Singleton beans are created, injected and initialised; bean post-processors create proxies and @PostConstruct methods run
The embedded web server starts, ApplicationRunner and CommandLineRunner beans run, and ApplicationReadyEvent is published

templates.question: What is the difference between @Component, @Service, @Repository and @Controller?
keyPoints: All four are @Component specialisations that component scanning registers as beans
@Service adds no behaviour; it documents the business-layer role
@Repository enables translation of persistence exceptions into Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy
@Controller marks a Spring MVC controller; @RestController adds @ResponseBody to every handler method
The specific annotations also let aspects and pointcuts target a layer

templates.question: Which bean scopes does Spring offer, and what goes wrong when a singleton bean depends on a prototype or a request-scoped bean?
keyPoints: singleton (the default, one instance per container), prototype (a new instance per lookup), and the web scopes request, session and application
A bean is instantiated, injected and initialised (@PostConstruct), and destroyed with the container (@PreDestroy); Spring does not destroy prototypes
A prototype injected into a singleton is created once, so the singleton always uses the same instance
Fix it with ObjectProvider (or @Lookup) to get a new instance per use, or with a scoped proxy for request or session beans
Singletons are shared by all threads, so they must be stateless or thread-safe

templates.question: A method annotated with @Transactional (or @Async, or @Cacheable) works when another bean calls it, but has no effect when another method of the same class calls it. Why?
keyPoints: Spring implements these annotations with a proxy that wraps the bean
Only calls that go through the proxy are intercepted
A call from inside the class (this.method()) bypasses the proxy, so no transaction, async execution or caching happens
Move the method to another bean, call it through the proxy (an injected self-reference), or use AspectJ weaving
By default proxy-based annotations are also ignored on private methods

templates.subtopic: Inversion of control and dependency injection
templates.question: After a refactoring, the application fails at startup because OrderService needs PaymentService and PaymentService needs OrderService. How would you resolve it?
keyPoints: Spring Boot refuses circular references by default, and constructor injection cannot resolve them
The cycle signals tangled responsibilities rather than a wiring problem
Extract the logic both need into a third bean, or invert one dependency with an interface or an application event
@Lazy on one injection point makes it start but hides the design problem; switching to field injection is not a fix

misconceptions: Values in application.properties cannot be overridden at deployment time
Profiles are a good place to keep production secrets in the repository
@Value is the best way to bind a group of related settings

templates.question: How does Spring Boot find its configuration, and how would you override a property for one environment without changing the build?
keyPoints: Properties come from many sources with a defined precedence: command-line arguments and environment variables override application.properties or .yml in the jar
A profile-specific file (application-prod.yml) overrides the default file when that profile is active
Relaxed binding maps an environment variable such as SERVER_PORT to server.port
Configuration files outside the jar (a config directory, spring.config.location or spring.config.import) override the packaged ones

templates.question: What are Spring profiles, and how would you use them to run with a local setup on your machine and a real database in production?
keyPoints: A profile is a named set of configuration and beans, activated with spring.profiles.active
application-{profile}.yml holds the properties of that profile
@Profile on a bean or configuration class registers it only when the profile is active
The profile is chosen per environment (an environment variable or argument), not hard-coded in the build
Secrets come from the environment or a secret store, not from profile files in the repository

templates.question: Your service has a dozen settings for calling a payment provider: base URL, timeouts, retries and an API key. How would you bind and validate them?
keyPoints: Bind them to a @ConfigurationProperties class or record with a prefix, which handles nested objects and types such as Duration
Add @Validated with Bean Validation constraints so that wrong values fail at startup
Register it with @EnableConfigurationProperties or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan and inject it where needed
This is clearer and safer than many separate @Value fields
The API key comes from an environment variable or a secret store

templates.question: In production the application still connects to the local database, although application-prod.yml has the production URL. What would you check?
keyPoints: Whether the prod profile is really active: the startup log lists the active profiles
Whether a source with higher precedence, such as the SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL environment variable or a command-line argument, overrides it
The file's name, location and YAML structure
The actuator env and configprops endpoints show which property source a value comes from

misconceptions: Returning JPA entities directly from controllers is fine
Every error should be returned as 500
@RestControllerAdvice handles exceptions of one controller only

templates.question: Walk through what happens inside Spring MVC when an HTTP request reaches a @RestController method, until the response is written.
keyPoints: Servlet filters, including the Spring Security filter chain, run first; then the DispatcherServlet receives the request
A HandlerMapping finds the controller method and a HandlerAdapter invokes it
Argument resolvers bind path variables, query parameters and the body (with an HttpMessageConverter such as Jackson for JSON) and run validation
The return value is serialised by a message converter chosen by content negotiation
Exceptions are turned into responses by exception resolvers such as @ControllerAdvice handlers

templates.question: How do you implement global exception handling for a Spring Boot REST API, and what should an error response contain?
keyPoints: A @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods maps exceptions to responses in one place
Each exception type maps to the right status: 400 for invalid input, 404 for a missing resource, 409 for a conflict, 500 for unexpected errors
Responses have one consistent body, such as RFC 9457 problem details (ProblemDetail): type, title, status, detail
Stack traces and internal messages are not exposed to clients
Unexpected errors are logged with a correlation id that the response can carry

templates.question: How do you validate a request body in Spring Boot, and what happens when validation fails?
keyPoints: Bean Validation constraints (@NotNull, @Size, @Email) on the request DTO and @Valid on the controller parameter
A failure throws MethodArgumentNotValidException, which Spring answers with 400 Bad Request
A @ControllerAdvice handler can return the field errors in a consistent format
Nested objects are validated only when the field is annotated with @Valid
Rules across fields or depending on stored data need a custom validator or a check in the service

templates.question: A REST endpoint that lists orders has become slow in production. How would you troubleshoot it?
keyPoints: Measure first: find where the time goes with metrics, traces or timed logs (Actuator and Micrometer, an APM tool)
Check the database work: SQL logging for N+1 queries, slow queries and their plans, missing indexes
Check the payload size and whether the endpoint paginates
Check downstream calls and pool saturation: database connection pool, HTTP client pool, server threads
Fix the bottleneck (fetch joins, indexes, pagination, caching) and confirm it with the same measurement

templates.question: Design the endpoint that creates an order: URL, method, request and response bodies and status codes, including what happens when the product is out of stock.
keyPoints: POST /orders with a request DTO, not the JPA entity, validated with Bean Validation
201 Created with a Location header and the created order as a response DTO
400 Bad Request with field errors for invalid input
409 Conflict (or 422) with a problem-details body when a business rule such as stock availability fails
Separate DTOs avoid exposing internal fields and lazy-loading problems

misconceptions: FetchType.LAZY guarantees that no extra queries are run
save() must be called for changes to a managed entity to be written
Derived query methods always produce efficient SQL
Open Session in View has no cost

templates.question: What is the N+1 query problem in JPA, how do you spot it, and how do you fix it?
keyPoints: One query loads N parent entities, then accessing a lazy association runs one more query per parent
SQL logging or Hibernate statistics show the same query repeated with different ids
Fix it per use case with JOIN FETCH, an @EntityGraph or a DTO projection query
Batch fetching (@BatchSize or hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size) reduces it to a few queries
Switching the association to EAGER is not a fix: it loads the data everywhere and can still cause N+1

templates.question: What is the persistence context in JPA, and why is a change to a managed entity saved without calling save()?
keyPoints: The persistence context (EntityManager or Session) tracks the entities loaded or persisted in a transaction, one instance per id
At flush, before commit or before a query, dirty checking writes the changes of managed entities as UPDATE statements
save or merge is needed only for new or detached entities
When the transaction ends the entities become detached and further changes are not tracked

templates.question: A controller that returns an entity throws LazyInitializationException: could not initialize proxy - no Session. What is happening, and how do you fix it properly?
keyPoints: A lazy association is touched, often during JSON serialisation, after the transaction and its persistence context have closed
The proxy cannot load its data without a session
Load what the use case needs in the service (JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph) and map it to a DTO inside the transaction
Do not return entities from controllers
Turning on open-in-view or EAGER fetching hides the problem and costs performance

templates.question: You need a paginated search over orders with optional filters on status, customer and date range. How would you implement it with Spring Data JPA?
keyPoints: Accept a Pageable and return a Page, or a Slice to avoid the extra count query
Build the optional filters with Specifications (Criteria API) or Querydsl instead of one derived method per combination
Index the filtered and sorted columns
Return DTO projections rather than whole entities
Sort by a stable, unique key so that pages do not overlap

misconceptions: @Transactional rolls back on every exception
@Transactional works on private methods
A transaction covers calls to other services
@Transactional alone prevents concurrent updates from overwriting each other

templates.question: How does @Transactional work in Spring, and what are its limitations?
keyPoints: Spring wraps the bean in a proxy whose interceptor starts or joins a transaction before the method and commits or rolls back after it
The transaction is managed by a PlatformTransactionManager and bound to the current thread
Only calls through the proxy are intercepted: self-invocation is not, and by default only public methods are
It covers one transactional resource, typically one database; calls to other services are not part of it
Work started on other threads does not take part in the transaction

templates.question: Which exceptions make a @Transactional method roll back by default, and how do you change that?
keyPoints: By default unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException) and Errors roll back
Checked exceptions commit by default
rollbackFor and noRollbackFor change the rules
An exception caught inside the method does not cause a rollback
When an inner transactional method marks the shared transaction rollback-only and the exception is swallowed, the commit fails with UnexpectedRollbackException

templates.question: What do the propagation settings REQUIRED and REQUIRES_NEW do, and when would you use REQUIRES_NEW?
keyPoints: REQUIRED (the default) joins the current transaction or starts one
REQUIRES_NEW suspends the current transaction and runs in a new one that commits or rolls back on its own
REQUIRES_NEW suits records that must survive the outer rollback, such as an audit log
It needs a second database connection while the outer one is held, which can exhaust the pool
NESTED uses a savepoint inside the same transaction instead

templates.question: A @Transactional service method throws an exception halfway through, but the rows it inserted before the exception are still in the database. What could cause that?
keyPoints: The exception is a checked exception, which does not roll back by default
The method was called from the same class, so the proxy and the transaction were bypassed
The exception was caught and not rethrown
The method is not public, or the object is not a Spring bean
The inserts ran in a separate transaction, for example a REQUIRES_NEW method

templates.question: Two users book the last seat of a flight at the same time and both succeed. The booking method is @Transactional. Why is the transaction not enough, and how would you fix it?
keyPoints: Under the default READ COMMITTED isolation both transactions read the seat as free before either writes
A transaction does not serialise concurrent transactions
Optimistic locking: a @Version column, and retry or fail on an optimistic lock exception
Pessimistic locking: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (@Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)) so the second booking waits
Or a conditional update (UPDATE ... WHERE available) or a unique constraint, checking the affected row count

misconceptions: A JWT is encrypted, so its contents are secret
CORS protects the server from malicious requests
Hashing passwords with SHA-256 is enough

templates.question: How does Spring Security authenticate and authorize an incoming request?
keyPoints: Requests pass through a servlet filter (FilterChainProxy) that selects the matching SecurityFilterChain
Authentication filters extract credentials (form login, HTTP Basic, a bearer token) and an AuthenticationManager with its providers verifies them
The result is stored in the SecurityContext, held per thread by the SecurityContextHolder
Authorization checks the rules (authorizeHttpRequests, @PreAuthorize) against the user's authorities
A missing or invalid authentication gives 401; an authenticated user without permission gets 403

templates.question: What are the trade-offs between server-side sessions and JWT access tokens for a REST API?
keyPoints: With sessions the server keeps the state and the client holds a session id cookie; revoking is easy
Scaling sessions needs sticky sessions or a shared session store
A JWT is a self-contained signed token that any instance can verify without a lookup
A JWT is hard to revoke before it expires, so access tokens are short-lived and renewed with refresh tokens
A JWT payload is only encoded and signed, not encrypted, so it must not carry secrets

templates.question: Users may only see and edit their own orders, and administrators may see all orders. How would you enforce that in a Spring Boot API?
keyPoints: Role checks for administrator endpoints at the URL or method level (hasRole, @PreAuthorize)
Ownership must be checked against the data: compare the order's owner with the authenticated user, or scope the query by owner
Answer another user's id with 404 or 403 consistently, without revealing whether it exists
Test that one user cannot reach another user's resources by changing the id (IDOR)

templates.question: A React app on localhost:5173 calls a Spring Boot API on localhost:8080. GET requests work, but POST requests fail with 403. What are the likely causes?
keyPoints: Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default and rejects state-changing requests without a CSRF token
For a stateless API authenticated by a bearer token CSRF protection can be disabled; with session cookies the token must be sent
The CORS preflight (OPTIONS) must be allowed and the origin configured in the security configuration, otherwise Spring rejects it
The browser console and the response tell a CORS failure apart from a rejection by the server

templates.question: How should a Spring Boot application store user passwords, and why?
keyPoints: Never in plain text or with reversible encryption
Use a slow, salted, adaptive hash such as BCrypt, Argon2 or PBKDF2 through a PasswordEncoder
The salt makes equal passwords hash differently and defeats precomputed tables
The work factor slows down brute force and can be raised over time
Fast hashes such as SHA-256 are unsuitable for passwords

misconceptions: @SpringBootTest is the right choice for every test
Mocking the repository proves that the query works
An in-memory database behaves like the production database

templates.question: What is the difference between @SpringBootTest, @WebMvcTest and @DataJpaTest, and when would you use each?
keyPoints: @SpringBootTest starts the whole application context (optionally a real server): realistic but slow
@WebMvcTest loads only the web layer and tests controllers through MockMvc with the services mocked
@DataJpaTest loads the JPA components and repositories, each test in a transaction rolled back at the end
Slices start faster and point failures to one layer

templates.question: How would you unit test an OrderService that calls a PaymentClient and an OrderRepository, including the case where the payment fails?
keyPoints: A plain JUnit test that passes Mockito mocks to the constructor; no Spring context is needed
Stub the payment client to succeed in one test and to throw in another
Assert the outcome and verify the important interactions, for example that the order is not saved as paid when the payment fails
Test behaviour rather than implementation details, and do not mock simple value objects

templates.question: Repository tests pass against H2, but the same queries fail in production on PostgreSQL. Why does that happen, and how would you change the tests?
keyPoints: H2 differs from PostgreSQL in SQL dialect, data types, functions, constraints and locking
Native queries and PostgreSQL features (jsonb, arrays, ON CONFLICT) behave differently or do not exist in H2
Run the integration tests against a real PostgreSQL with Testcontainers
Apply the same schema migrations (Flyway or Liquibase) in the tests as in production

templates.question: How do you decide what to cover with unit tests and what with integration tests in a Spring Boot service?
keyPoints: Unit tests cover business logic in isolation: fast, numerous and precise when they fail
Integration tests cover wiring and boundaries: queries, the HTTP layer, serialisation, transactions and security configuration
Mocks cannot show that real infrastructure behaves as assumed
Many unit tests, fewer integration tests and a few end-to-end tests (the test pyramid)
